notes: Meta (Menlo Park, founded 2004 as Facebook, renamed Meta in 2021) hasn't published a fixed, numbered 'Leadership Principles' document the way Amazon has. The 'leadership_principles_behavioral' dimension below is instead built around Meta's own well-documented cultural themes — the 'Move Fast' / 'Focus on Impact' / 'Be Bold' / 'Be Open' / 'Build Social Value' values from its 2012 IPO letter ('The Hacker Way'), plus the newer 'Meta, Metamates, Me' value introduced in 2022 (see worker/src/prompts.ts's META_VALUES) — candidates should be evaluated on whether their story genuinely demonstrates one of these themes, not on reciting a slogan.
1 = very weak / almost no evidence; 3 = moderate / acceptable; 5 = very strong / model answer.
Feedback tone: strict but constructive, like a coach who genuinely wants you to get the offer.

product_sense.name: Product Sense / Product Design
question_examples: How would you improve Reels to help it compete more effectively with TikTok?
Design a feature to help people discover and join relevant Facebook Groups.

clarity_and_structure.description: Whether the answer has clear assumptions, a game plan, and a clearly segmented structure (framing how they'll break down the problem up front, rather than jumping straight to a solution).
good_signals: Opens by restating the problem, clarifying goals and constraints, and making explicit assumptions where needed.
States their process up front, e.g.: person first, then pain points, then solution + metrics.
Every paragraph has a clear topic sentence with natural transitions.
bad_signals: Jumps straight into listing solutions or features with no framing at all.
Rambles with no paragraph structure, reads like stream of consciousness.
Never signals which part of the answer they're currently in (e.g. user, problem, solution).

scoring_guide.1: No structure at all — the answer is scattered and hard to follow.
scoring_guide.3: Has basic structure but inconsistent — some sections are clear, others jump around.
scoring_guide.5: Clearly structured throughout, like walking the interviewer through a design process step by step.

customer_obsession_and_motivation.description: Whether the answer explains why this product/problem matters starting from the person using it — for Meta, specifically tying back to the stated mission of giving people the power to build community and bring the world closer together, not just engagement for its own sake.
good_signals: Clearly describes the situation, relationships, and motivations of a specific type of person (e.g. a parent in a local Groups community, a creator building a Reels following) rather than a generic 'users'.
Connects concrete behavior and emotion with framing like 'If I were this person scrolling Feed at the end of a long day, what I'd actually want is...'.
Ties back to Meta's long-term relationship with people across its family of apps (trust, authentic connection, not just time spent).
bad_signals: Starts purely from engagement/revenue metrics with no discussion of the human experience at all.
Uses vague language like 'provide a better experience' without defining what 'better' means.
Ignores the specific value of Meta's family of apps to people, e.g. staying close to friends and family, finding community, discovering creators.

scoring_guide.1: Barely mentions the person using the product, or only in very generic terms.
scoring_guide.3: Has basic user framing but not concrete or situational enough.
scoring_guide.5: Genuinely feels like they understand a specific type of Meta user's life and concrete motivations.

segmentation_and_focus.description: Whether users/use cases are reasonably segmented, and whether the candidate picks one clear focus to go deep on — relevant for Meta since a single app like Facebook or Instagram spans teenagers, parents, small businesses, and creators with very different needs.
good_signals: Lists several possible user segments (e.g. casual scrollers, active creators, Groups admins, small business owners) and explains why their needs differ.
Clearly picks one primary segment and explains why (impact, fit, underserved).
All subsequent problem framing and solutioning stays aimed at that segment, without drifting to others.
bad_signals: The whole answer talks about 'all users' with no real focus.
Segments are defined too superficially (e.g. only by age/region) without connecting to motivation and behavior.
Keeps switching the target audience mid-answer, so the story falls apart.

scoring_guide.1: No segmentation at all — fully one-size-fits-all.
scoring_guide.3: Some segmentation attempted but unclear, or the reasoning for the chosen focus is weak.
scoring_guide.5: Segments are clear and mutually exclusive, and the answer stays consistently focused on the chosen one.

problem_identification.description: Whether the candidate genuinely understands and concretely describes the person's problem to solve, rather than jumping straight to a feature.
good_signals: Describes the pain point with a concrete scenario/example, e.g. exactly where in a flow (discovering a Group, browsing Marketplace, watching Reels) people drop off or get frustrated.
Distinguishes between a 'want/wish' and an actual 'blocker/problem'.
Connects the problem to its impact (e.g. lower return visits, reduced sharing, lost trust in recommendations).
bad_signals: Treats a feature request as the problem itself, e.g. 'there's no better recommendation algorithm, so we need one'.
Describes the problem too abstractly to imagine happening to a real person.
Lists a pile of problems with no prioritization.

scoring_guide.1: Doesn't show what specific problem is actually being solved.
scoring_guide.3: Lists a few reasonable problems, but not deep enough or unprioritized.
scoring_guide.5: Problem is concrete and prioritized, and directly drives the design decisions that follow.

solution_quality_and_tradeoffs.description: Whether the proposed solution has enough depth, a clearly scoped v1, and trade-offs that fit Meta's scale and its ads-funded, engagement-sensitive business model.
good_signals: States the high-level solution direction first, then breaks it into a few key experience/feature modules.
Clearly defines v1 vs. future extensions, showing judgment about what to ship first.
Calls out risks and downsides (e.g. effects on time spent, content quality, creator incentives, or ad load) and explains how to mitigate them.
bad_signals: Throws out ideas like a feature list with no connection or prioritization.
v1 tries to do too much, unrealistic given resources and time-to-value.
Never mentions any risk, failure mode, or constraint — e.g. ignores that a change could hurt content diversity or creator trust.

scoring_guide.1: Solution is scattered or clearly unrealistic.
scoring_guide.3: Has a roughly reasonable direction, but v1 scope / trade-offs are unclear.
scoring_guide.5: Proposes a convincing, practical v1 and clearly explains why it's designed that way.

analytical_execution.name: Analytical / Execution / Metrics
question_examples: How would you measure the success of Meta AI inside Messenger?
Daily active usage of a Facebook Group feature dropped 15% after a redesign. How would you investigate?

goal_definition.description: Whether the candidate clearly defines what goal or success state the problem is meant to achieve.
good_signals: Clearly distinguishes input vs. output metrics.
Asks up front, 'What are we actually trying to optimize for — engagement, retention, monetization, or meaningful social interaction?'.
Connects back to Meta's long-term value: authentic connection, time well spent, and the ad-funded business model that depends on both.
bad_signals: Jumps straight into listing KPIs without explaining why they're the right ones.
Fixates on a single metric (e.g. raw time spent) with no consideration of balance or side effects.
Never addresses the tension between engagement and meaningful/healthy usage.

metric_selection_and_reasoning.description: Which metrics are chosen, why, and whether there are guardrail metrics.
good_signals: Proposes 1-2 north star metrics (e.g. DAU/MAU, meaningful social interactions) paired with 3-5 supporting/guardrail metrics.
Explains what user behavior or business outcome each metric represents.
Considers trade-offs, e.g. short-term engagement vs. long-term retention and trust.
bad_signals: Piles on metrics arbitrarily with no prioritization.
Chosen metrics aren't actually measurable or aren't related to the problem.
Forgets qualitative/behavioral metrics related to content quality or well-being.

structured_debugging_and_hypotheses.description: When facing an anomalous metric, whether the candidate systematically hypothesizes causes and designs ways to validate them.
good_signals: First distinguishes whether this is a tracking/instrumentation issue vs. a real behavior change.
Hypothesizes in layers (ranking algorithm change / UI redesign friction / seasonality / a competing app pulling attention away).
Proposes concrete experiments or analysis methods to validate (A/B tests, cohort analysis, funnel breakdown by platform/region).
bad_signals: Guesses at causes purely on intuition with no systematic breakdown.
Forgets to rule out instrumentation/logging errors.
Never proposes any concrete way to validate a hypothesis.

prioritization_and_tradeoffs.description: Given multiple possible solutions or experiments, whether there's a clear prioritization.
good_signals: Prioritizes using an impact vs. effort/risk framing.
Accounts for Meta's scale (billions of users, many markets and languages) rather than greedily trying to do everything at once.
Explains why a given experiment goes first, and what the next step is if it fails.
bad_signals: Treats every idea as equally high priority.
Doesn't consider execution cost, technical risk, or rollout risk at Meta's scale.
Picks their favorite idea with no clear reasoning.

leadership_principles_behavioral.name: Leadership Principles / Behavioral
question_examples: Tell me about a time you had to move fast and ship something imperfect rather than wait for a perfect solution.
Describe a time you had to make a bold call that other people on your team disagreed with.

story_structure_star.description: Whether the story is told clearly using a STAR / STAR+ structure, rather than a rambling description.
good_signals: Clearly states Situation / Task / Action / Result, ideally with a Reflection as well.
Every part has a clear timeline and clearly defined roles.
The result is concrete, with numbers or an observable change.
bad_signals: Everything is blended together — unclear what the problem was, what they did, and what the result was.
The result is vague, e.g. 'everyone was happy' with no concrete evidence.
The story is too short or shallow, like routine day-to-day work.

ownership_and_decision_making.description: Whether the candidate shows accountability for outcomes and proactively elevated their perspective to make decisions, rather than just executing instructions.
good_signals: Clearly states they proactively identified the problem or proposed the solution, rather than being assigned it.
Explains their own role in the key decision, including the risk and consequences they owned.
Pushed back / exercised influence when facing resistance, rather than passively accepting it.
bad_signals: The whole story sounds like they were just following someone else's plan.
Blames the problem or failure entirely on other people or circumstances.
No evidence of long-term thinking anywhere in the story.

alignment_with_specific_lp.description: Whether the story actually demonstrates a specific Meta value (e.g. Move Fast, Be Bold, Focus on Impact — see worker/src/prompts.ts's META_VALUES), rather than just claiming 'this shows X'.
good_signals: The action details themselves show the theme in practice, e.g. for Move Fast, concretely describing shipping a scoped v1 and iterating rather than waiting for certainty.
Connects to the spirit of the value, rather than just reciting a label.
Reiterates the lesson learned in the result or reflection section.
bad_signals: Only says 'this is Focus on Impact' at the start or end of the story, with no evidence in the middle.
Crams in too many values at once, so each one is weakly supported.
The story content actually contradicts the claimed value, e.g. claiming Move Fast while the whole story is about an extended, risk-averse review process.

reflection_and_learning.description: Whether there's genuine reflection on the experience, and an explanation of how behavior changed afterward.
good_signals: Admits there were things they could have done better, not afraid to name a real misstep.
States a concrete, observable behavior change (e.g. how they'd scope a bolder v1 earlier next time, or build better guardrails before moving fast).
Ties the reflection back to a Meta value or broader career growth.
bad_signals: The 'lesson learned' is vague, e.g. 'communicate more'.
No reflection at all — just showcasing success.
The reflection is unrelated to the actual story.

strategy_business.name: Strategy / Business Thinking
question_examples: How should Meta think about competing with TikTok for younger users' attention over the next 3 years?
Should Meta prioritize further investment in Threads, or focus resources on strengthening Instagram and Facebook instead?

structured_market_and_customer_analysis.description: Whether market, competition, and customers are analyzed in a structured way, rather than just a pile of buzzwords.
good_signals: Starts by roughly scoping the market (TAM/SAM/SOM is fine at a rough level) across social/short-video/messaging.
Clearly describes the differences and needs across target user groups (e.g. teens, young adults, parents, small businesses, creators).
Identifies key competitors/alternatives (TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, X/Threads' own competitors, iMessage) and Meta's relative strengths and weaknesses.
bad_signals: Just says the market is big or growing fast, with no structure at all.
Ignores Meta's existing capabilities and family-of-apps distribution, as if this were a brand-new startup.
Recites business-school frameworks with no real connection to Meta's actual context.

meta_ecosystem_and_network_effects_fit.description: Whether the strategy accounts for how Meta's actual growth loop works: more people and content on one app (e.g. Instagram) can drive signups and engagement on another (e.g. Threads, WhatsApp) through cross-posting, shared identity, and shared contact graphs, and whether it accounts for the ads-funded business model where engagement and advertiser demand are both required for the strategy to be sustainable.
good_signals: Discusses how the strategy affects engagement, content supply (from creators), and the advertiser-facing side of the business, not just the end-user side.
Explains how this strategy reinforces (or is reinforced by) Meta's family of apps — shared login, cross-posting, contact graph — or its 2023-2026 push into Meta AI and generative ad tools.
Considers the impact on creators and advertisers, not just casual users.
bad_signals: The strategy could apply to any social app — nothing Meta-specific (its family-of-apps distribution, ads business model, creator ecosystem) is addressed.
Ignores the advertiser/monetization side entirely, only talks about end users.
Only discusses short-term engagement, no consideration of long-term trust, content quality, or regulatory risk.

prioritization_and_roadmapping.description: Whether the strategy can be broken down into an actionable roadmap with a clear sequence.
good_signals: Proposes 2-3 main strategic directions, each broken into milestones or initiatives.
Accounts for resource constraints and risk, clearly stating what comes first and what comes later.
Describes how each strategic direction's success would be tracked with metrics.
bad_signals: Stays very high-level with no concrete execution steps at all.
The 'roadmap' is just a timeline with no real strategic thread connecting it.
Ignores risks and dependencies (e.g. regulatory scrutiny, platform policy, cross-team coordination).

estimation.name: Estimation / Guesstimate
question_examples: Estimate how many Reels are watched globally per day.
How many small businesses actively use Click-to-WhatsApp ads in a given month?

assumption_clarity.description: Whether every assumption made is clearly stated, and whether the candidate checks that it's reasonable.
good_signals: States the key assumptions (user base size, penetration rate, frequency, etc.) before calculating.
Assumptions are logically consistent with each other, not contradictory.
Willing to adjust an assumption when needed, and explains why.
bad_signals: Throws out numbers with no stated source.
Realizes partway through that an earlier assumption was wrong, but doesn't fix it.
An assumption is clearly unreasonable (e.g. every user watches 100 Reels a day).

problem_breakdown_and_math.description: Whether the problem is reasonably broken down and the math comes out roughly correct.
good_signals: Breaks the big problem into a few dimensions (user base x penetration rate x frequency x average session value, etc.).
The calculation process is orderly and clearly narrated out loud.
Sanity-checks the final result to see if it looks reasonable at Meta's billions-of-users scale.
bad_signals: The breakdown is disorganized or double-counts the same group of people.
Gets lost partway through without reorganizing the steps.
No sanity check at all.

communication_and_poise.description: Whether the candidate stays calm and clear while estimating out loud, and how they handle uncertainty.
good_signals: Narrates their thinking while calculating, so the interviewer can follow along.
When uncertain, is willing to say 'there are two ways to break this down, I'll go with this one first'.
Doesn't get thrown off entirely by a small mistake.
bad_signals: Panics the moment a calculation error is noticed, and the whole answer falls apart.
Never verbalizes their thought process, so it's unclear how they're thinking.
Obsesses over precise decimal points, losing sight of the big picture.

system_design.name: System Design / TPM
question_examples: Design the ranking system that decides what shows up in someone's News Feed.
Design a system to detect and limit the spread of misinformation across Meta's family of apps.

requirements_and_scoping.description: Whether the candidate clarifies functional and non-functional requirements (scale, latency, consistency, who the users are) before proposing a design, rather than designing in a vacuum.
good_signals: Asks about scale (daily active users, posts/requests per day), latency expectations (feed must load near-instantly), and consistency needs up front.
Clarifies which use cases are in scope for v1 vs later (e.g. one app vs. the whole family of apps).
States explicit assumptions when the interviewer doesn't provide a number.
bad_signals: Jumps straight into naming technologies/components with no sense of scale or constraints.
Never distinguishes must-have requirements from nice-to-haves.
Ignores who actually uses the system and why.

high_level_architecture.description: Whether the candidate proposes a clear, sensible breakdown of the system into major components and explains how data/requests flow between them.
good_signals: Breaks the system into a small number of clear components (e.g. candidate generation, ranking model, serving, feedback logging) with a simple story for how they connect.
Explains the role of each component in plain language before naming any specific technology.
Keeps the design at the right altitude for a PM/TPM — enough structure to reason about trade-offs, not a line-by-line engineering spec.
bad_signals: Describes components with no explanation of how they interact.
Gets lost in low-level implementation detail (specific model architectures, exact schemas) instead of the overall shape.
The design doesn't actually address the stated requirements.

scalability_and_tradeoffs.description: Whether the candidate identifies where the design would break under scale and reasons about real trade-offs (e.g. freshness vs. ranking quality, personalization vs. diversity, cost vs. latency).
good_signals: Identifies the most likely bottleneck (e.g. real-time ranking at billions of requests/day, a hot content item going viral) and proposes a fix.
Explicitly names a trade-off and picks a side with a reason, rather than listing pros/cons with no decision.
Considers cost and engineering effort, not just theoretical scalability.
bad_signals: Treats the system as if it will always run at small scale with no failure modes.
Lists trade-offs without ever committing to a recommendation.
Adds complexity (e.g. a new ranking signal) without justifying why it's needed.

operational_and_cross_team_thinking.description: Whether the candidate addresses how the system would be monitored, rolled out safely, and delivered in practice — including working with engineering, integrity/policy, and other teams, which is central to the TPM angle of this question type.
good_signals: Mentions how they'd monitor health (key metrics/alerts, e.g. prevalence of bad content, feed load time) and detect failures after launch.
Describes a staged rollout (e.g. internal dogfood, small percentage, then full launch across the family of apps) rather than a single big-bang release.
Talks about which teams (engineering, integrity/trust & safety, legal/policy) need to be involved and where dependencies or risks lie.
bad_signals: The design ends at launch with no mention of what happens operationally afterward.
No acknowledgment that other teams or dependencies exist.
Ignores failure handling entirely, as if the system will never go down or be gamed.

ai_pm.name: AI Product Manager
question_examples: Design how Meta AI should proactively suggest replies inside a Messenger conversation.
How would you decide whether a new Feed ranking model is ready to launch to everyone?

problem_ml_fit.description: Whether the candidate first establishes that the problem genuinely calls for an ML/AI solution — and what that solution needs to be good at — rather than assuming AI is the answer by default.
good_signals: Asks what a non-ML solution (rules, heuristics, chronological ordering) would look like and explains concretely why ML does better here.
Identifies what the model actually needs to predict or generate, in plain language, before discussing data or architecture.
Considers user trust and explainability implications of using AI for this specific problem (e.g. why someone is seeing a given post or suggestion).
bad_signals: Assumes 'use AI' is the answer without explaining what problem it solves better than a simpler approach.
Confuses the AI feature with the product goal, e.g. treats 'add a generative AI assistant' as the goal itself.
Never considers whether a simpler, faster-to-ship solution would work almost as well.

data_and_evaluation_strategy.description: Whether the candidate thinks concretely about what data the model needs and how they would measure whether it's actually working, both offline and after launch.
good_signals: Names the specific data/labels needed and where they'd realistically come from (e.g. engagement signals, explicit feedback, human-rated samples).
Proposes concrete offline metrics (e.g. precision/recall, relevance) AND online/business metrics (e.g. meaningful interactions, time well spent), and explains why both matter.
Considers what 'good enough to ship' looks like, not just 'best possible model'.
bad_signals: Never mentions data at all, as if the model appears fully trained.
Picks a single vague metric like 'engagement' with no connection to the business or user outcome.
Confuses model-quality metrics with product success metrics, or never distinguishes them.

responsible_ai_and_risk.description: Whether the candidate proactively considers failure modes, bias/fairness, misinformation, and safety risks the AI feature could introduce at Meta's scale, and how to guard against them.
good_signals: Names a concrete failure mode (e.g. biased content ranking, hallucinated Meta AI responses, unfair treatment of a demographic group) specific to this feature.
Proposes a concrete guardrail: human review, confidence thresholds, fallback to a non-AI path, or a way to catch bad outputs before they reach billions of people.
Considers user trust, misinformation spread, and how a visible AI mistake would affect Meta's reputation.
bad_signals: Treats the model as if it will never be wrong.
Mentions 'responsible AI' only as a buzzword with no concrete mechanism.
Ignores the specific risk profile of this feature (e.g. misinformation, youth safety, privacy).

iteration_and_feedback_loops.description: Whether the candidate describes a realistic plan for launching, monitoring, and improving the AI feature over time, including how model drift and user feedback are handled.
good_signals: Describes a staged launch (e.g. shadow mode, small percentage rollout in one market) before a full launch across the family of apps.
Explains how they'd detect the model degrading over time (drift, changing content trends, adversarial behavior) after launch.
Describes a concrete feedback loop, e.g. using user actions or explicit feedback (likes, hides, reports) to retrain or tune the model.
bad_signals: Treats the launch as the finish line with no plan for what happens after.
Never mentions how they'd know if the model gets worse over time.
No mechanism for turning real-world usage back into model improvement.
